title: Serving Runtime — Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Runbooks
author: Ava Martinez
content:
Summary
-------
This document consolidates the serving runtime reference for Redwood Inference: architecture overview, kernel scheduling design, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, recent release notes, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended for engineers owning runtime improvements, SREs on-call for inference services, and performance-focused applied-ML teammates who onboard models for production.

Scope
-----
Covers core production runtime components: inference-gateway, smart-router, batchd (batch dispatcher), rdw-runtime nodes, kvcache, and observability/tracing. Includes:
- Design and constraints that guide kernel selection and scheduling.
- Profiling recipes (tools, commands, and interpretation).
- Benchmarking suite description and recommended workloads.
- Release notes for the active stable release.
- Known issues and mitigation guidance.
- Runbooks for common incidents (high tail latency, OOMs, degraded throughput).

Architecture overview
---------------------
High-level components
- inference-gateway (HTTP + gRPC endpoints): authentication, request validation, quota checks.
- smart-router: routes requests by policy (latency, cost, region, tier), primary implementation in Go (service: smart-router).
- batchd (batch dispatcher): aggregates requests by model variant and target sequence length; performs dynamic batching and dispatch to runtime nodes.
- rdw-runtime (runtime node): GPU process hosting kernels, KV cache integration, and local scheduler. Daemon name: rdw-runtime-daemon.
- kvcache: distributed prefix & KV cache (service: kvcache-cluster), exposes Redis-compatible API for cache hits.
- metrics & tracing: Prometheus exporters + OpenTelemetry collector (service: telemetry-collector).

Design constraints and principles
- Latency SLOs prioritized over absolute throughput for customer-facing hosted API.
- Cache correctness: strong read-after-write semantics for pinned model variants.
- Deterministic kernel selection for reproducible perf profiles across regions.
- Graceful degradation: automatic fallback to compatible model variants (quantized / smaller).

Kernel selection and scheduling model
-----------------------------------
Goal: map an incoming batch to the optimal kernel implementation and GPU resource allocation that meets latency SLOs while maximizing tokens/sec.

Key concepts
- Kernel profiles: precomputed performance table for (model-arch, sequence-length, batch-size, hardware-type, quantization). Stored in model-catalog as JSON blobs named profile-<model>-<hw>.
- Scheduling unit: a dispatch group defined by (model-variant, seq-bucket, priority).
- Cooperative scheduling: rdw-runtime uses a lightweight cooperative scheduler to interleave generation and KV serving for multi-tenant workloads.
- Preemption: high-priority (SLA) requests can preempt queued low-priority batches within configured limits.

Default scheduling policy (recommended)
1. Route -> group by model-variant, target tokens (seq-bucket), and customer tier.
2. Select kernel variant using score = latency_penalty * w1 + tokens_per_sec * w2 + memory_headroom_penalty * w3. (Weights tuned in model-catalog).
3. If expected p99 latency > SLO, route to lower-cost/reduced-precision variant or spill to dedicated pool.
4. Apply dynamic batching with max_batch_size and latency-bound timer.

Example default thresholds (tunable via config service):
| metric                   | default value | notes |
|-------------------------|---------------|-------|
| max_batch_size          | 32            | per-GPU soft cap for gpus with 80GB vram |
| batching_latency_ms     | 8             | timer to close batch (milliseconds) |
| kvcache_hit_rate_target | 0.75          | below this, recompute cache policies |
| p99_short_seq_slo_ms    | 200           | short sequences (<=64 tokens) |
| p99_long_seq_slo_ms     | 1200          | long sequences (>=512 tokens) |

Profiling playbook (step-by-step)
---------------------------------
Purpose: produce reproducible profiles that isolate kernel hotspots, memory growth, and synchronization stalls. Follow these steps in a staging cluster or a dedicated profiling node.

Prerequisites
- Access to profiling nodes (label: profiling=true).
- Docker images: rdw/rdw-runtime:profiling and telemetry-collector.
- Tools: NVIDIA Nsight Systems (nsys), NVIDIA Nsight Compute (ncu), nvidia-smi, python torch.profiler, perf, and pprof for Go services.

Steps
1. Reproduce the workload with a workload driver (scripts/bench/run_driver.py) using a fixed seed and recording request traces: 
   - example: python scripts/bench/run_driver.py --model gptx-2b --seq 64 --concurrency 16 --tokens 20000 --out workload.json
2. Capture system-level trace: nsys profile --sample=cpu,cupti --output=nsys_report \
   --trace=nvtx,cuda -- nvprof not recommended for Ampere+.
3. Capture kernel-level metrics: ncu --target-processes=all -o ncu_report --metrics sm__throughput.avg,dram__throughput.avg --pid <pid>.
4. Capture PyTorch operator timeline (if model uses torch): insert torch.profiler in model server with schedule and use tensorboard to inspect. Example snippet included in scripts/profiling/torch_profiler_example.py.
5. Collect logs and flame graphs for Go services: go tool pprof -http=:6060 /tmp/pprof.cpu.prof.
6. Analyze cache behavior: collect kvcache metrics (kvcache.hit_rate, kvcache.latency_50/95/99). If hit_rate < 0.6, inspect prefixing logic.

Interpretation checklist
- High kernel occupancy but low SM throughput -> memory or warp divergence issue.
- High cudaMemcpy time -> check host-to-device pinning and batching alignment.
- Frequent small kernels -> consider kernel fusion or operator grouping.
- Large gaps between kernel launches -> synchronization or mutex contention in runtime.

Benchmarking suite
------------------
Overview
- The benchmarking suite (repo: infra/benchmarks/serving) drives end-to-end scenarios and microbenchmarks. Bench jobs produce artifacts: latency histograms, tokens/s, cost_estimate.csv, and prom-metrics bundles.

Workloads (canonical)
- chat-short: 8-132 tokens, prompt-heavy, used for p50/p99 SLO validation.
- chat-medium: 64-1256 tokens, typical chat assistant workload.
- chat-long: 512-10248 tokens, generation-heavy workloads for memory-pressure testing.
- embedding-batch: embedding models, batched inference with large batch sizes to measure throughput.

Metrics captured
- p50/p90/p99 latency (ms) per request
- tokens/sec and tokens/dollar (cost model uses spot price + power cost)
- GPU utilization, memory high-water mark, and kernel-level occupancy
- KV cache hit rate and cache latency

Running a benchmark (example)
1. Deploy benchmark infra stack: scripts/bench/deploy.sh --cluster staging-bench --profile benchmark
2. Run canonical workload: scripts/bench/run_suite.sh --suite chat-short --repeat 5 --out results/chat-short/
3. Summarize: python scripts/bench/summary.py --dir results/chat-short --format html

Quality gates and SLOs
- Recommended commit gate: new model variants must pass benchmark suite and show no more than 5% regression in tokens/sec and p99 latency versus baseline.
- Production SLOs: availability >= 99.95%, p99_short_seq < 200ms (hosted), p99_long_seq < 1200ms.

Release notes (v1.8.0, 2026-03-10)
----------------------------------
Highlights
- Kernel selection library: added flash-attention-v2 optimized kernels for GPT-like attention (avg 18% tokens/sec improvement on A100/RTX8000).
- Cooperative scheduler: experimental rollout for multi-tenant inference to reduce p99 by up to 12% under mixed workloads.
- Profiling image: rdw/rdw-runtime:profiling-1.8.0 with torch.profiler hooks and nsight-friendly symbols.
- Observability: added kvcache hit-rate dashboard and automated regression alert thresholds.

Bug fixes
- Fixed memory leak in rdw-runtime when using seq_bucket > 1024 (issue #4231).
- Resolved deadlock between batchd and smart-router for backpressure signals (issue #4278).

Upgrade notes
- Rolling upgrade recommended: 10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100% with 30-minute hold for perf validation.
- When rolling back, clear local KV caches on runtime nodes to avoid stale prefix mismatches: kubectl exec -n infra -c rdw-runtime <pod> -- /usr/local/bin/clear_kvcache.sh

Known issues (top consumer-facing items)
-------------------------------------
- ISSUE-5012: intermittent p99 spikes for long sequences on RTX8000 with mixed precision. Mitigation: pin model to alternative quantized variant or move heavy customers to dedicated pool. Root cause under investigation (vectorized GEMM path).
- ISSUE-4987: rare OOM when multiple long-seq requests hit the same GPU. Mitigation: adjust max_batch_size and enable early spill to disk in rdw-runtime config.
- ISSUE-4901: profiling builds can cause ~5% perf regression vs release build; use production builds for final perf numbers.

Operational runbooks
--------------------
Runbook: High tail latency (p99 above SLO)
1. Acknowledge page and follow incident playbook; notify #sre-serving-runtime and @oncall-runtime.
2. Check Grafana dashboard: service -> rdw-runtime -> p99 by seq_bucket.
3. Determine scope: single zone vs cluster-wide. If single node, SSH to node and run: nvidia-smi -q -d MEMORY; kubectl logs -c rdw-runtime <pod> --since=15m
4. If kernel stalls suspected, capture temporary nsys trace on the affected runtime pod: kubectl exec -it <pod> -- nsys profile --output=/tmp/nsys_report.nsys --trace=nvtx,cuda -- <start-command>
5. Apply mitigation: reduce max_batch_size on affected node(s) or route traffic to fallback quantized variant via smart-router rule. Example CLI: curl -X POST $ROUTER_ADMIN/api/routes/fallback -d '{"model":"gptx-2b","variant":"int8-fallback"}'.
6. If broad regression after deploy, roll back to previous release following Upgrade notes.
7. Post-incident: attach artifacts (nsys_report, logs, metrics snapshot) to incident and create regression ticket with perf regression summary.

Runbook: OOM on runtime node
1. Identify OOM by kube events and rdw-runtime logs (OOMKilled).
2. Inspect pod resource usage: kubectl top pod <pod> -n infra.
3. Check recent deploys for changed model variants or new model onboarding.
4. Temporarily cordon node: kubectl cordon <node>; migrate pods to nodes with more memory or dedicated pool.
5. Increase swap/spill threshold: update ConfigMap infra/rdw-runtime-config map key memory_spill_threshold -> 0.65 and rollout.
6. If persistent, create a hotfix: reduce max_batch_size for offending model-variant and schedule model-level quantization.

Ownership and escalation
- Primary owners: serving-runtime team (team alias: eng-serving-runtime).
- On-call: see rotations in /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-and-incident-response (alias: @oncall-runtime).
- Escalation path: oncall -> runtime tech-lead -> eng-sre lead -> CTO.

Team wiki and onboarding checklist
- Links
  - Runtime repo: git.internal/redwood/rdw-runtime
  - Bench repo: git.internal/redwood/infra/benchmarks/serving
  - Observability dashboards: Grafana -> infra/serving-runtime
  - Oncall runbook: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/postmortems/runbook-runtime

Onboarding checklist (new runtime engineer)
1. Read this document and the runbooks.
2. Clone rdw-runtime and run local unit tests.
3. Run a small end-to-end benchmark in staging (chat-short).
4. Shadow on-call for 2 weeks and resolve at least one paged incident.
5. Attend kernel-scheduling design review.

Appendices
----------
A. Example rdw-runtime config fragment (yaml)
- NOTE: the actual file lives in infra/rdw-runtime-config; below is a simplified example.

```
# rdw-runtime-config fragment
max_batch_size: "32"
batching_latency_ms: "8"
memory_spill_threshold: "0.65"
kvcache_enabled: "true"
kernel_selection_profile: "model-catalog/profile-gptx-2b-a100.json"
```

B. Useful commands
- Restart batchd on a node: kubectl rollout restart deployment/batchd -n infra
- Clear local KV cache: kubectl exec -n infra -c rdw-runtime <pod> -- /usr/local/bin/clear_kvcache.sh
- Run a quick microbenchmark: scripts/bench/microbench.sh --model gptx-2b --seq 64 --batch 8
